July 2025Webster Pass, Colorado

Webster Pass

memories below

Iron Basin

Mountains can rust. I learned that over the Fourth of July weekend, camped in the high basins east of Montezuma, an old mining town just up the valley from Keystone. A rough 4x4 road climbs toward Webster Pass (leave the sedan at home), and up there the slopes turn red, orange and ocher. The color is iron: rain and snowmelt slowly rust the rock, and the stain runs downhill until it meets water. Near camp sat a tarn, a small mountain lake whose water was clear and green-turquoise, with shallows that glowed orange along the edge. I assume that's more of the same iron.

The drone showed me the rest, and every photo below is a still pulled from its video. From the air the road zigzagged across a rust-brown mountainside beneath a snow-streaked peak. Snow still clung to the shaded faces, and one long white tongue of it ran down a green ridge, in July! A stream spilled down terraces of maroon rock, ringed by spruce. Off to one side, a storm cloud dragged rain across the far ranges in long gray streaks, and on the horizon a flat silver glint might have been Dillon Reservoir. I flew until the light went low and warm.

After dark the sky over the tarn filled with sharp stars. The road is a pencil line, the tarn a green coin, and the iron has been rusting these slopes for far longer than anyone has driven up them. The snow will probably wander off down the Snake River past Keystone and into the reservoir. The red isn't going anywhere.
